challenges.headline: Undefined recipient roles
challenges.premise: The request assumes 'the right people' is self-evident and can be resolved later.
challenges.alternative: Route notifications through the Client's Contact roles (operational, billing) the platform already models, with the mapping configurable per client, rather than inventing a fixed recipient list for this feature alone.
challenges.consequence: Hardcoding a guessed recipient set risks alerting the wrong person or missing the account manager/freelancer entirely — the exact failure the feature exists to prevent — and forces a rebuild the first time a client wants different routing.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm recipient roles and whether routing varies by client before writing the trigger logic; design against the existing Contact-role model rather than a bespoke list.

challenges.headline: Static end-date trigger
challenges.premise: The request implies a one-time scheduled check against a fixed mission end date.
challenges.alternative: Treat the end date as mutable: re-evaluate or reschedule the alert whenever the mission is extended, renewed or ended early, and explicitly cancel any pending alert tied to a superseded date.
challenges.consequence: Without this, alerts fire on stale end dates after a renewal, or fail to fire after an early termination — producing exactly the missed-follow-up problem the feature is meant to solve, plus noisy false alerts that train recipients to ignore them.
challenges.recommendation: Design the trigger to recompute on every mission update, not as a fire-once scheduled job against a frozen date.

challenges.headline: Notification scope vs invoicing automation
challenges.premise: The request frames this as 'notify people,' but the domain tightly couples mission end to final invoicing.
challenges.alternative: Scope this phase strictly to the alert itself — a notification with a link to the mission — and treat any automatic final-invoicing or offboarding trigger as a separate, later-phase decision with its own amount-sourcing and idempotency rules.
challenges.consequence: If invoicing automation gets folded in implicitly, the build inherits invoice numbering, amount-sourcing and idempotency concerns mid-stream, without ever having been scoped or estimated.
challenges.recommendation: Get explicit client sign-off that phase one is notification-only, with invoicing/offboarding automation deferred to a follow-up.

decisions.decision: Mission-end alerts are computed via a scheduled/asynchronous check rather than fired synchronously off a mission edit
decisions.why: The trigger is a future-dated condition (approaching end date), not an immediate state change, so it naturally fits a periodic evaluation rather than an inline event.
decisions.alternative: Check on every mission save and compute whether it's within the alert window at that moment.
decisions.tradeoff: A scheduled check adds a small latency window and requires a job scheduler, but avoids re-running alert logic on every unrelated mission edit.

challenges.headline: Fire-and-forget notification, no follow-through
challenges.premise: The request assumes sending a notification is the finish line — success is defined as 'the alert went out.'
challenges.alternative: Model this as a tracked reminder with a status (pending/seen/actioned) against the mission, so an ignored alert can escalate instead of silently expiring like today's missed check.
challenges.consequence: Without tracking, this just swaps 'nobody checked the calendar' for 'nobody read the email' — the same failure mode, and there's no way to measure whether it actually reduced missed renewals since no success metric is defined either.
challenges.recommendation: Define the success metric with the client first, then decide whether the feature needs an acknowledgment/escalation loop or is genuinely just a one-way alert.

challenges.headline: Single global lead-time threshold
challenges.premise: The request treats 'about to end' as one fixed trigger point, with no mention of it varying.
challenges.alternative: Build the threshold (and possibly staged reminders — e.g. 30 days then 7 days) as a per-client/contract configurable rule from the start, since this platform's business rules routinely vary that way.
challenges.consequence: Hardcoding one global threshold now means reopening the trigger engine later the first time a client asks for a different lead time — expensive to retrofit on a platform built around client-specific rules.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether the threshold must be configurable per client/contract before building the trigger logic.

challenges.headline: Isolated trigger vs. existing end-of-mission event
challenges.premise: The request scopes this as a new, standalone 'notify' feature, but the context already treats mission-end as an event other automation (final invoicing, validation) subscribes to.
challenges.alternative: Attach this notification as another subscriber to whatever end-of-mission event mechanism already (or will) handle final invoicing, rather than building a second, parallel date-watcher with its own idempotency rules.
challenges.consequence: Two independent mechanisms reacting to the same mission end-date changes doubles the places where extension/cancellation logic can drift out of sync, and duplicated or missed triggers become harder to debug.
challenges.recommendation: Check whether Missions already has (or plans) an end-date-change event bus for final invoicing, and hook into it rather than building a separate scheduler.

challenges.headline: Static alert vs. a moving end date

challenges.alternative: Recompute the alert dynamically whenever the mission's end date changes, instead of scheduling a one-time job off the date captured at creation time — mission end dates are explicitly called out as something that moves via renewal or early cancellation.
challenges.consequence: A naive single-shot scheduler produces stale, duplicate or missing alerts the moment a mission is extended, ended early, or renewed — exactly the scenario this feature exists to catch.
challenges.recommendation: Define the recompute/cancel logic for date changes and an idempotency rule before touching the scheduler design.

challenges.headline: Notification-only vs. offboarding automation
challenges.premise: The request is framed as 'notify people,' but end-of-mission is a known trigger point on this platform for final invoicing and access revocation, and the model already flags this ambiguity without resolving it.
challenges.alternative: Scope this build strictly to the alert itself, and treat final-invoice drafting or access revocation as a separate, explicitly agreed follow-on — chaining them in silently turns a notification into a mission close-out workflow.
challenges.consequence: Unscoped, the feature can quietly grow from a simple reminder into an orchestration engine touching Invoicing and permissions, without anyone having priced or approved that scope.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client, in writing, whether this phase is notification-only or the first slice of a broader mission-end workflow.
